public_rationale: Measured workplace gains contradict the categorical denial of substantive enhancement beyond social-media testimonials [e1]. A peer-reviewed study published February 27, 2026 reported a pooled 26.08% increase in completed tasks across three randomized workplace experiments involving 4,867 developers in 2022–2023 [e1]. Results differ by setting: METR found 19% longer completion times among 16 experienced developers using February–June 2025 tools on familiar projects [e2]. Its February 24, 2026 update said selection effects and measurement problems made its follow-up an unreliable estimate of current productivity effects [e3]. These findings establish enhancement in some workplace settings, without establishing universal gains [e1, e2, e3].
limitations: The studies do not settle whether the tools are very expensive or whether most costs are hidden from users or paid by employers [e1, e2, e3].
The positive study used company-run experiments and includes a Microsoft-affiliated author [e1].
Completed-task gains do not establish broad worker replacement, overall software quality, maintenance costs or profitability [e1].
The early-2025 slowdown is not a reliable estimate for July 2026 tools [e2, e3].

our_interpretation: The plain reading of the enhancement clause denies demonstrated, meaningful gains in real work beyond social-media testimonials.
A substantial measured workplace productivity gain can contradict that blanket denial without proving widespread replacement or profitability.
The word 'yet' makes the achievement claim cumulative through July 28, 2026; the target therefore includes earlier workplace experiments.
For the ongoing cost component, June 2026 is the latest completed monthly reporting period before publication.
'Most' requires a defined population and more than half of relevant costs; employer payment and provider subsidy are different quantities.
The Twitter description is treated as a contrast with credible workplace evidence, not a literal personality classification.
criteria.support_condition: Representative cost evidence establishes the stated majority burden, while credible workplace evidence supports the absence of meaningful enhancement or replacement through the post date.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Credible real-work evidence establishes meaningful enhancement beyond testimonials, contradicting the categorical enhancement clause; alternatively, representative cost records contradict the majority-cost assertion.

evidence.publisher: INFORMS / Management Science, abstract deposited with Crossref
evidence.explanation: The abstract reports a pooled 26.08% increase in completed tasks across three workplace experiments involving 4,867 developers. The original paper dates the experiments to 2022–2023; this is meaningful workplace enhancement, although task counts do not establish overall software quality or profitability.

A randomized study of 16 experienced developers working on familiar repositories found slower completion with early-2025 tools. This supports skepticism about benefits in that setting, but cannot establish that meaningful enhancement has never occurred elsewhere.

METR cautions that selection effects and measurement problems make its follow-up an unreliable estimate of current productivity effects. The early slowdown should therefore not be presented as a settled estimate for July 2026 tools.
